canonical_statement: AFFIRM compared long-term rate-control and rhythm-control treatment strategies in patients with atrial fibrillation at high risk of stroke or death.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: randomized, multicenter comparison of these two treatment strategies

canonical_statement: Eligible patients were at least 65 years old or had other risk factors for stroke or death, with atrial fibrillation judged likely to recur and warrant long-term therapy; anticoagulation could not be contraindicated.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Patients who were at least 65 years of age or who had other risk factors for stroke or death could be enrolled

inclusion_criteria: Age >=65 years or other risk factors for stroke or death

canonical_statement: The rhythm-control strategy allowed cardioversion and protocol-approved antiarrhythmic drugs selected by the treating physician to maintain sinus rhythm.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Attempts to maintain sinus rhythm could include cardioversion as necessary

exposures.details: Cardioversion as needed plus physician-selected protocol antiarrhythmic therapy intended to maintain sinus rhythm.

canonical_statement: The rate-control strategy used beta-blockers, verapamil or diltiazem, digoxin, or combinations, targeting heart rate <=80 beats/min at rest and <=110 beats/min during a six-minute walk.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The goal was a heart rate not higher than 80 beats per minute at rest

exposures.details: Ventricular rate control with beta-blockers, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin, or combinations; protocol rate targets <=80 bpm at rest and <=110 bpm during 6-minute walk.

canonical_statement: Warfarin was targeted to an INR of 2.0-3.0; continuous anticoagulation was mandated in rate control, whereas in rhythm control it could be stopped at physician discretion after sustained apparent sinus rhythm.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The goal for anticoagulation with warfarin was an international normalized ratio (INR) of 2.0 to 3.0

canonical_statement: The primary endpoint was overall mortality.
